entry.title: What does Aloe Vera do in PEAK?
entry.summary:
PEAK's Mesa update has added plenty of new items to the game, and Aloe Vera is one of the most important items to find to survive the new biome.
One of the harshest aspects of the new biome is the element of heat, especially during the day. If you're not careful enough, the heat can make you faint and jeopardize your chances of going past this level and continuing your ascent to the top.
That's where Aloe Vera can be of great use when you are trying to keep your body temperature down to save yourself in the Mesa biome.
Table of contents How does Aloe Vera work in PEAK? How to find Aloe Vera in PEAK?
How does Aloe Vera work in PEAK?
There are certain items like the Sunscreen that works as a preventive measure. It stops your body temperature from going up when you're exploring the Mesa biome. But the temperatures will rise, and you might not have enough Sunscreen to begin with. Aloe Vera allows you to to bring down your body temperature if it has risen to dangerous levels.
Screenshot by Destructoid
The item is also directly related to completing the Cool Cucumber badge. This badge requires you to pass Mesa while maintaining your Heat below 10 percent. If your Heat is at the border, you can quickly consume Aloe Vera to reduce the temperature before taking shelter.
How to find Aloe Vera in PEAK?
Unlike most of the new items added to PEAK, Aloe Vera is found in the open. I've never seen it in the luggage lying around on the island. You'll typically find them near cactuses in the Mesa biome. It might not always spawn beside a cactus, but it's pretty common in my experience.
That's pretty much all you need to know about Aloe Vera in PEAK. Make sure to collect as much as possible as they're relatively light and can be extremely useful in hazardous situations.

entry.title: Apex Legends' latest go at a compressed battle royale forgets the journeying spirit at the genre's heart
entry.summary: Apex Legends launched its Season 26 update this week with the new Wildcard mode, what must be its fourth or fifth attempt at a 'battle royale but faster' sideshow. If anything, Wildcard – with its tightened safe zones, generous respawn allowances and automatic loot pickups – is the most ferocious, cage fightin'est variant yet, its matches routinely playing out as breathless slaughters as crammed-in squads fight, die, and resurrect over a condensed selection of strongholds. Still, while I’ve enjoyed ApeLegs' previous action-favouring tweaks, something about Wildcard underwhelms. It’s not the shooting, which is as crisp and dynamic as in any other Respawn FPS. And it’s not the simplified gear gobbling, which is fine for a supplementary mode. It’s that at the end of a Wildcard round, even the ones I’ve won, I’ve never felt that I’ve really gone anywhere or done anything except aim down my sights and left-click. entry.title: I was a fool for skipping Widelands, the only game as good as The Settlers
entry.summary:
Between fifty game releases a day, and among them official successors and open source remakes, most 90s games your grandma bangs on about have some modern equivalent that somewhat fills the gap.
But not The Settlers. There hasn't been a Settlers game since 1996. Whether they were good or not, its many sequels, as early as 3, started missing the point of the design. It's the roads, man. The roads!
This isn't about iconography for its own sake. It's a design thing, an ethos. The heart of The Settlers was that your towns lived or died based largely on how well you designed your transport logistics. It was all about the roads. It doesn't even fit into a genre really, let alone the lopsided RTS the sequels collapsed into. It sounds like a typical town builder, especially today when there's a wealth of games about placing a woodcutter and a farm, but I'm tempted to say it's not even about gathering resources.
